sources.names.institutions: The place's own bodies, generic types. Town bodies carry the town's name: a town council (Local Government Act 1972 parish and town councils; the principal authority being North Yorkshire Council, E06000065), a building society, the town's own police neighbourhood team, health centre and primary school. Real national bodies at the right level are used where the town has none of its own: HM Land Registry (land registration, Land Registration Act 2002), the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber) (rents and leasehold disputes; possession claims are in fact heard in the county court), the Housing Ombudsman Service (Housing Ombudsman Scheme). Source for these: general knowledge of English institutions and gov.uk (not opened for each); the names of the town's own bodies are invented.

sources.culture.conducts: What people start out holding right, for the four conducts where a figure in this profile's own outlook speaks to it (the rest start from values alone: no figure was opened). approves_bps is the national share with 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot' of confidence, as `outlook.trust` has it (World Values Survey and European Values Study, joint wave 7, as Our World in Data publishes it; opened 2026-10-11, to confirm against the survey's tables; see sources.outlook for the country and the items). Mapping, ours: answer_tribunal and take_to_tribunal <- confidence in the courts (a person who trusts the courts approves of answering a case there and of taking a wrong to it); complain <- confidence in the civil service (writing to the town is approved where the town's officers are trusted to answer); join_union <- confidence in labour unions. Weak: confidence in an institution is not approval of an act toward it, and the share above a threshold is read as a mean, as outlook does; the figure sets where people start (their own lean and their picture of what others approve), nothing else, and the lean is measured from it, so the rates stay the calibrated ones. No figure for strike, take_in, stay_past_notice, take_from_employer or an organisation's conduct (the survey's items on joining strikes and on the justifiability of stealing property were not opened); no figure by origin group (no source found that gives one). National, not the place's. does_bps is never given: a conduct's own rate in the profile.

sources.tenancy.rent_share_of_income: PLACEHOLDER bands around a mean read from a summary: private renters in England spent on average 34% of gross household income on rent counting housing support as income, 39% without it; by income fifth 63, 40, 28, 21 and 17%; 71% of private renters in the lowest two fifths spent over 30% (MHCLG, English Housing Survey 2023-24, headline findings chapter 2 and the rented sectors report, https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/chapters-for-english-housing-survey-2023-to-2024-headline-findings-on-demographics-and-household-resilience/chapter-2-housing-costs-and-affordability, read through a fetch summary on 2026-10-12: to confirm; one fetch gave other figures). No bands are published in the chapters; the bands here (24% under a fifth, 26% a fifth to three tenths, 32% three tenths to a half, 18% over a half) are a placeholder shaped to that mean. To replace from the survey's annex tables. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/generator.md, "Homes by income"): each renting household of a new town draws its share from these bands (evenly within a band; the open band from its lower bound to twice it, at most everything), which gives the rent it carries; households and let homes are matched by it. A target as well: the town's own distribution at the start is reported beside it and is not fitted to it.
sources.support.take_up_bps: PLACEHOLDERS. pension 95%: the State Pension is near-universal by design; 13.1 million received it in Great Britain in February 2025 (DWP benefits statistics August 2025, opened 2026-10-12) and no population of 66 and over was opened to divide by. unemployment 60%: DWP publishes no take-up estimate for Universal Credit; 1.6 million people on it were searching for work in July 2025 against about 1.67 million unemployed (a search summary), groups that do not match. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/generator.md, "Payments in force"): of those the payment's rule already entitles as the year begins, this share open with it in payment; the rest claim it when they first look, as before. 2026-10-16: DWP's take-up estimates cover pensioner benefits only (Pension Credit about 63%, a means-tested benefit, not the State Pension) and none exists for Universal Credit; nothing here replaces either figure.
sources.ownership.owner_bps_by_age: Owner-occupiers by age of the household reference person, England, 2023-24: 17% at 16-24, 45% at 25-34, 71% at 55-64 (MHCLG, English Housing Survey 2023-24, headline findings chapter 1, https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/chapters-for-english-housing-survey-2023-to-2024-headline-findings-on-demographics-and-household-resilience/chapter-1-profile-of-households-and-dwellings, opened 2026-10-12). The bands 35-54 and 65 and over were not in the chapter (Annex Table 1.4, not opened): 35 to 54 is read at the 25-34 figure and 65 and over at the 55-64 figure, which understates both. To replace from the annex table. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/generator.md, "Homes by income"): only as how much likelier a household of one age is than another to be among the town's owners; their number is the houses the profile's house_owner_bps makes owner-occupied.
sources.households.kin_households_most_bps: 3.58%: 'Other household types', 9,814 of 274,381 households in North Yorkshire (ONS, Census 2021, TS003 Household composition, via Nomis NM_2023_1, https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/api/v01/dataset/NM_2023_1.data.csv?geography=E06000065, opened 2026-10-12). The category holds multi-family households and also students and unrelated sharers, so it is an upper bound for households that hold kin. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/households.md, "Taken in"): a ceiling and nothing else: no more households than this hold kin when people with nothing coming in are placed with a household that can carry them.
sources.tenancy.possession: Housing Act 1988 s 8 and Schedule 2 ground 8: at least two months' rent unpaid, on four weeks' notice; a possession order usually takes effect 14 days on; a warrant is carried out by county court bailiffs (to confirm: recalled, the Act not opened; the Renters' Rights Act, in force 1 May 2026, changes the grounds). plan_months 6 (courts suspend possession on terms to pay: no figure) and warrant_days 42 are PLACEHOLDERS (the median time from claim to repossession was 26.4 weeks in January to March 2026: Ministry of Justice, opened). The two shares of how tenants answer are the same in every profile: stay_past_notice_bps 5000 is a PLACEHOLDER (no figure was found for the share of tenants who stay past a notice for arrears); leave_on_order_bps 5900 is England's, used everywhere: of 16,848 landlord possession orders in January to March 2026, 6,888 repossessions were by county court bailiffs, 41%, so about 59% of those ordered out were gone without one (Ministry of Justice, Mortgage and Landlord Possession Statistics, January to March 2026: opened by a research agent for this work, 2026-10-11; a ratio of one quarter's flows, not of one cohort). eviction_notice_days: the notice of the day that whoever carries out a warrant gives the tenant; England's county court bailiffs give 14 days' notice of an eviction (Civil Procedure Rules 83.8A: to confirm, recalled), Germany's Gerichtsvollzieher about three weeks (to confirm); every other place's figure is a PLACEHOLDER (7 days; Ohio 3, within its ten). HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/justice.md, "Possession"): published in the town as a law; a landlord gives a notice to vacate under it, applies to the tribunal if the tenant stays, and asks for a warrant if they stay past its order; the tribunal sets a plan or a date by it; the police carry the warrant out. Tenants who answer, and plans (2026-10-12): answer_bps 4000 is a PLACEHOLDER: 'most tenants do not attend' (MHCLG, Factors influencing housing case progress and outcomes in county courts, 2018, s 5.1.2.4, opened 2026-10-12), and about 60% of hearings with neither tenant nor a lawyer for them (secondary, not opened). plan_consider 'may' and plan_barred_rent_months 2: on a discretionary ground the court may adjourn, or suspend or postpone possession, on conditions as to payment of the arrears (Housing Act 1988 s 9, opened 2026-10-12); it has no such power on the mandatory ground of two months' rent owed at the notice and at the hearing (Schedule 2, ground 8: recalled, to confirm). 2026-10-16 (source check): arrears_days 91 (was 56) and plan_barred_rent_months 3 (was 2): after the Renters' Rights Act 2025 (in force 1 May 2026) ground 8 needs at least THREE months' rent in arrears at the notice and at the hearing, on four weeks' notice (law-firm and Shelter summaries returned by search; legislation.gov.uk Schedule 2 was fetched but did not show the ground: SUMMARY-ONLY, to confirm). The earlier two months was the law before 2026. notice_days 28 stands. possession_days 14, plan_months 6 and warrant_days 42 are still placeholders as above.
sources.business.entry_bps_per_year: ONS, Business demography, UK: 2024: birth rate 11.1% of active businesses, death rate 9.8%; five-year survival of 2019 births 38.4% (opened by a research agent for this work, 2026-10-11). United Kingdom; England alone not retrieved. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/entry.md, "Starting a business of one"): the generator turns it into a monthly chance for those who could start a business of one (in the labour force, of working age, with the savings for its stock), from the businesses the town has: births a year at this rate, over those people. Most real births are businesses with no employees, which is the only kind that can be started here without premises.
sources.employment.hours: Employment Rights Act 1996 Part XI (ss 147-154, lay-off and short-time working; legislation.gov.uk opened in summary 2026-10-13): an employer may lay off or put on short time only if the contract allows it; otherwise it needs agreement. A guarantee payment of a daily amount (about 41 pounds from April 2026 to confirm) for up to 5 days in 3 months (ss 28-35) is owed and not modelled (it is small against a month's pay); an employee on lay-off or short time for 4 or more weeks in a row, or 6 in 13, may claim redundancy pay (s 148) and is not modelled. The 40-hour week is a placeholder. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Hours before heads"): published in the town as a law (law-cutting-hours); a shop or factory over its need cuts everyone's hours to what its trade needs before it lets anyone go, where this says it may, and pays what it owes for the hours cut; a worker reads the employer's paper as the pay agreed. consent_bps 9000 is a PLACEHOLDER (of workers asked to agree to a cut as the alternative to someone being let go, the share who do; no figure found). The employer's own notice of 3 days is ours, so that the paper reaches the worker first. 2026-10-16: ss 28-35 guarantee pay opened: GBP 41 a day from April 2026, up to 5 days in 3 months (s 31), matching the figure above, still not modelled; s 148 (4 or more weeks in a row, or 6 in 13, with written notice within 4 weeks) opened and agrees. What ss 147-154 say is when lay-off and short-time count, and that pay depends on the contract; that an employer may not cut hours without a contract right is the law of contract, not Part XI's text, so 'consent' rests on the common law (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1996/18/section/147, opened 2026-10-16). consent_bps 9000 and ordinary_week_hours 40: still placeholders (no figure found).
sources.employment.adjustment: PLACEHOLDERS, the same in every profile, with a sourced shape (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Adjusting labour"; docs/research/references.md). smooth_months 3: firms plan production and workforce on smoothed, forecast trade and not on the last period's (Holt, Modigliani, Muth and Simon 1960); no figure for the horizon of a small employer here was found. hiring_cost_weeks 8: what recruiting and training a new worker costs, in weeks of their pay; estimates run from under two weeks to over sixteen (Silva and Toledo 2009; Manning 2011; Blatter, Muehlemann and Schenker 2012; Muehlemann and Leiser 2018: all to confirm, none opened), and none is for this place.
sources.employment.termination: Employment Rights Act 1996 s 86 (notice: a week after a month's service, then a week for each year to twelve) and s 162 (redundancy payment after two years: a week's pay for each year of service at ages 22 to 40, half below and one and a half above, to twenty years; one week a year is used for every age, and the cap on a week's pay is left out) (to confirm: recalled by a research agent for this work, 2026-10-11, the statute not opened). HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Adjusting labour"): published in the town as a law; an employer reads it before letting someone go for redundancy (what it would owe is part of what the job costs to end) and pays what it says when the job ends. Service is counted from the start of a run: nobody's earlier years with an employer are known to it. 2026-10-16: the statute is now opened. s 86: one week after a month's service, one week for each year from 2 to 12 years, 12 weeks at 12 or more: the table above agrees. s 162: a redundancy payment of 1.5 weeks per year of service aged 41 and over, 1 week aged 22 to 40, 0.5 week under 22, counting back at most 20 years; the weekly pay cap is GBP 751 from 6 April 2026 (search; not applied); the profile's one week a year for every age stands as a simplification (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1996/18/section/86 and /section/162, opened 2026-10-16).
sources.frictions: Everyday frictions (docs/behaviour/frictions.md): what goes wrong, how often, and how the bodies that hear it work. Read by the generator only for a town whose spec has `living`.
sources.frictions.per_adult_bps_per_year: Of adults, the share who had each kind of problem, a year: half the share who had it in the last two years in World Justice Project, Global Insights on Access to Justice 2019 (General Population Poll 2017-18, about 1,000 respondents a country; the summary statistics workbook was opened; national, and for Brazil and Mexico the three largest cities only). landlord: a problem with a landlord over agreements, payments, repairs, deposits or eviction (9.2% in two years; all of it is given to disrepair here, which overstates repairs: the town has no other landlord problem of the kind yet). wages: difficulty obtaining wages or employment benefits agreed in advance (3.0%). bill: major disruption of a utility's supply or incorrect billing (12.1%; all of it is given to wrong bills). benefits: difficulty obtaining public benefits or government assistance (7.0%). goods: a consumer problem (29.3%) less the utility share, since the survey's consumer problems include it (derived; poor professional services are in it too). The generator turns each into a rate for those exposed (a let dwelling, a job, a customer, a claim) with the town's own counts. Halving a two-year share understates a yearly one where people have a problem in both years (to confirm against a yearly survey). 2026-10-16 (source check, NOT applied): wages 150 happens to equal the ONS share of employee jobs paid below the minimum wage, 1.5 to 1.6% in April 2025 (447,000 jobs; ONS, Low and high pay in the UK: 2025, opened), a stock of jobs at a point in time that ONS says is not a measure of non-compliance: a different definition, the match is coincidence. bill 605: water companies had 205,853 household complaints in 2024-25, 63% about billing (about 0.6% of households, CCW), energy billing about 30% of supplier complaints; complaints, not wrong bills, so not comparable.
sources.frictions.put_right_on_asking_bps: Asked to put it right, how often the other side does. goods: 56% of consumer problems ended positively (Consumer Protection Study 2022, opened); the rest: PLACEHOLDERS standing at the share of people with any problem who say it is done and fully resolved (45.9%: World Justice Project, Global Insights on Access to Justice 2019 (General Population Poll 2017-18, about 1,000 respondents a country; the summary statistics workbook was opened; national, and for Brazil and Mexico the three largest cities only)), which is an outcome of everything people tried, not the rate at which the other side agrees when asked: to replace with a figure by kind of problem. 2026-10-16 (not applied): the Housing Ombudsman upheld some maladministration in 71% of 7,082 determinations in 2024-25 (annual complaints review, search summary); that is an outcome after escalation, not how often a thing is put right when asked.

sources.frictions.support: (Until foundations F6 this note also gave a processing time, a placeholder fortnight, and a daily capacity; both are gone: how long a claim takes is the hours of whoever decides it.) wrong_refusal_bps: of claims that qualify, the share wrongly refused. FITTED in the 1,000-person town of the first profile (7% of qualifying claims gives about as many refusals a year as 6% of adults, its survey share with difficulty obtaining public benefits, counting the refusals that are right), and for every other place scaled by its own survey share against that one: a stand-in until a place's own rate of decisions changed on review is found. 2026-10-12: this fit assumed every entitled person claims in the year. A town now opens with the payments its people are already entitled to in force (granted before the year, never decided in it), so it decides fewer claims and refuses fewer (Victoria 37.8 to 24.8 a year). It is NOT re-fitted: that would be fitting an outcome again. sources.support.payments: [The pension:] New State Pension, full rate, GBP 241.30 a week from April 2026 (4.8% rise under the triple lock; GOV.UK / DWP benefit and pension rates 2026-27; search summaries, to confirm) = GBP 482.60 a fortnight. [The payment to those out of work:] Universal Credit standard allowance, single claimant aged 25 or over, GBP 424.90 a month from 7 April 2026 (DWP, benefit and pension rates 2026-27; search summary, to confirm) = GBP 196.11 a fortnight (x12/26). SHAPE (2026-10-08, track D of docs/design/profile-depth.md): support is now a list of payments, each a rule in three parts: who qualifies, how much, for how long (docs/behaviour/boundary.md); the law is published and the payments office reads it. The payments for those out of work end the year before the profile's retirement age (to_age): the rule the generator applied to every profile until now, written into the payment, where it can be changed. Two payments, the same figures: nothing is changed. Still left out, as this note says: Universal Credit's means test and taper and its housing and child elements (a means test on declared household income, `who.income_under`, and sums for a household's members and children can now be said; the taper cannot: a payment that falls as income rises is not built).

sources.labour_force_share_by_age: ILOSTAT, 'Labour force participation rate by sex and age (%)', five-year bands (dataflow DF_EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT, https://sdmx.ilo.org/rest/data/ILO,DF_EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT/all?startPeriod=2019; the data file opened and these figures read from it, 2026-10-08), persons, the United Kingdom, national, annual 2025, from the ONS Labour Force Survey: ages 25 to 54, 87.434%; 55 to 59, 76.772%; 60 to 64, 60.117%; 65 and over, 13.141%. The profile's own participation figure (labour_force_participation_bps) still says how many are in the labour force at the reference ages; this curve says only how that share falls with age.

sources.public_finance.income_tax: Income tax 2026-27, England: personal allowance GBP 12,570 (frozen until 2031), basic rate 20% to GBP 50,270, higher rate 40% to GBP 125,140, additional rate 45% above (GOV.UK, Income Tax rates and Personal Allowances; to confirm for 2026-27). The levy is National Insurance (employee Class 1 main rate 8% from the primary threshold of GBP 12,570, which is 2% above GBP 50,270; thresholds frozen; GOV.UK 'National Insurance rates and categories', to confirm). The personal allowance taper (lost at GBP 1 per GBP 2 above GBP 100,000), the 2% rate on high earnings and employers' National Insurance (15% above GBP 5,000) cannot be expressed. Employers deduct tax through PAYE on cumulative pay; the profile reckons each pay as a year's income. SHAPE (2026-10-08, track E of docs/design/profile-depth.md): the law is now a list of charges, each with what it is charged on, its schedule, its reliefs and whom it is paid to (docs/behaviour/public-finance.md). Income Tax, the same figures said as the law says them: the personal allowance of GBP 12,570 taken off the pay, and the rates on what is left (20% on the first GBP 37,700, which is GBP 50,270 less the allowance; 40% to GBP 125,140; 45% above). EXPRESSED NOW, from this note: the allowance tapering away at GBP 1 for each GBP 2 of pay above GBP 100,000 (no wage in the profile is near it). UN-FOLDED: the levy of 8% of the whole of a pay from GBP 12,570 that stood for National Insurance is now the contribution as this note gives it: 8% of pay between the primary threshold of GBP 12,570 and GBP 50,270, and 2% above, paid to National Insurance and not to general revenue. That lowers what is withheld from every wage by 8% of GBP 12,570 a year. Not expressed: employers' National Insurance (a charge the employer bears is not built).

It does a share of the task 'serve' (scope: placeholder, 30%, in the range of the share of a retail worker's tasks that Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock 2023 find exposed to current systems; to confirm) in as long as a person takes (placeholder). production-cell: an automated line or cell: set-up about US$90,000 for a cell (the installed cost of an industrial robot system is a few times the robot's price of about US$50,000: International Federation of Robotics, World Robotics; to confirm), a yearly licence and maintenance about 10% of it, five years' licence, a fifth of the set-up to leave; it does 35% of the task 'make' (placeholder) in 70% of a person's time (placeholder). oversight_hours_per_month and error_bps are placeholders (what looking after one costs the buyer's own staff; how often it gets a unit wrong, refunded at the unit's price). case-handling-system: a system that writes an office's routine papers (a rates notice, a permit decision) and records them: set-up about US$40,000 and a yearly licence of 30% of it (a public-sector case-management system's price; placeholder, to source), three years' licence, a fifth of the set-up to leave; it writes them in 15% of a clerk's time (placeholder) and can do 60% of them (placeholder, in the range Eloundou et al. 2023 give for clerical work; to confirm). sources.automation.firms: How a business weighs a system (docs/behaviour/automation.md). payback_months: the months over which the costs of changing (set-up, exit) must be repaid, 24 for a small business and 36 for a large one (ten staff or more): placeholders, in the range firms report requiring for equipment of two to three years (Graham and Harvey 2001, 'The theory and practice of corporate finance', Journal of Financial Economics; to confirm). hurdle_bps: the margin by which the saving must beat the cost, 20% (placeholder, a margin of safety for a manager's own estimate being unsure). reference_bps: each business already using it that the vendor names eases the hurdle by 2 points, never below nothing (Mansfield 1961, 'Technical change and the rate of imitation', Econometrica; Griliches 1957; Rogers 2003: uptake follows how many have taken it up; the size is a placeholder). on_cost_bps: what staff cost beyond their wage, 0: the world models no employer's charges beyond the wage and redundancy pay. most: the most systems of one kind it takes at once (placeholder).
